newsitem.title: USA: Reno told in May about China campaign allegations.
newsitem.headline: Reno told in May about China campaign allegations.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno said on Thursday she learned last May of allegations China was trying to pass money to U.S. election candidates and she believed at the time that the White House had been properly informed.

Reno said a "misunderstanding" between the FBI and White House National Security Council aides was to blame for the information not actually reaching President Bill Clinton, and said she had ordered a review of the procedures involved.

Her comments followed contradictory statements by Clinton and the FBI on the issue earlier this week, after the White House insisted the president had not been informed of the claims -- which China has strongly denied -- until recently.
Campaign contributions from foreign governments are illegal.

The issue was a further blow to the White House as it struggled with accusations of improper fundraising from Asian interests by the president and his Democratic Party in his campaign for re-election last year.

Reno told a regular weekly news conference that the FBI told her last May about possible Chinese efforts to funnel money to congressional candidates in the elections. Several members of Congress were also briefed on the allegations.
After the FBI advised her in May, Reno said it had been decided that she would call then-White House National Security Adviser Tony Lake to tell him about the allegations.
"I was not able to reach Lake, and told them (the FBI) to make sure the briefing went forward and assumed that the briefing would take place -- that everybody would be briefed," she said.
Reno said she never talked to Lake because the June briefing took place and she thought at the time the information went to the appropriate people at the White House.
"I thought it was serious enough. We had the FBI advise the White House," Reno said.

She repeated her explanation about the "misunderstanding." She said that at the June briefing of two mid-level White House National Security Council aides, the FBI agents placed no restrictions on disclosing the information to other officials, but did say it involved a sensitive matter.
The two NSC aides took this general caution to mean they could not pass along the information to higher-ups.

"I believe I should have known," Clinton told reporters on Monday, the same day the White House and the FBI engaged in a rare public disagreement on whether any restrictions had been placed on disseminating the information.
Pressed on whether Clinton should have been told, Reno replied, "I think the National Security Council should be determining what the president should know or not know."
She said the Justice Department and the FBI would conduct the internal review looking into briefings involving classified information to the White House and Congress.
"I'm just troubled whenever there appears to be a misunderstanding. That's why I want to review it and make sure that we have clear communication lines," she said.

With investigations into Clinton's fundraising tactics under way in Congress and by the FBI, The Washington Post reported on Thursday that four planned White House receptions for wealthy Democratic contributors had had been cancelled.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry took issue with the report, which said the action was taken for fear of aggravating the fund-raising controversy. He said the events had never been locked into Clinton's schedule.
"They were never planned for the White House," he said, adding that Clinton aides declined to schedule some events at the White House until new fund-raising rules were in place.

In Congress, Representative Spencer Bachus, an Alabama Republican who toured China with two other Republican lawmakers in December, said he should have been warned by the FBI of China's alleged attempts to influence U.S. policy before he accepted the free trip.
And a House Judiciary Committee spokesman said committee Republicans were sending Reno a letter demanding she seek an independent counsel to probe the fund-raising controversy.

Reno has steadfastly rejected such requests, maintaining there has been no "specific, credible evidence" of a criminal violation that would trigger the independent counsel law. Her Justice Department is investigating the allegations.
